claim: The ability to generate ripplet oscillations in response to a synchronous thalamocortical volley can be used as a stringent 'reality check' for existing computational models.
source: This will accelerate development of detailed, biologically grounded computational models of the neocortical network; indeed, the ability to generate ripplet oscillations in response to a synchronous thalamocortical volley can now be used as a stringent 'reality check' for existing models (Banitt et al., 2007; Markram et al., 2015; Hass et al., 2016; Gouwens et al., 2018; Borges et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of ripplets for validating computational models.

claim: Studies of neocortical ripplets are likely to shed new light on the synaptic mechanisms underlying similar oscillations in other brain areas, such as hippocampal ripples.
source: Studies of neocortical ripplets are also likely to shed new light on the synaptic mechanisms underlying similar oscillations in other brain areas, such as hippocampal ripples.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of studying ripplets.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

source: Thalamocortical brain slices (Agmon and Connors, 1991; Porter et al., 2001) of somatosensory (barrel) cortex, 300–350 μm thick, were cut in same solution using a Leica VT-200 vibratome and placed in a submersion holding chamber filled with recirculated and oxygenated ACSF (in mM: NaCl 126, KCl 3, NaH2PO4 1.25, CaCl2 2, MgSO4 1.3, NaHCO3 26, and D-glucose 20).
evidence: This is a description of the slice preparation methods.

source: Slices were incubated for at least 30 min at 32°C and then at room temperature until use.
evidence: This is a description of the slice preparation methods.

source: For recording, individual slices were transferred to a submersion recording chamber and continuously superfused with 32°C oxygenated ACSF at a rate of 2–3 ml/min.
evidence: This is a description of the recording conditions.

claim: Upon strong depolarization, FS cells invariably reached steady-state firing rates of 150–300 Hz and their spike trains showed no or little frequency adaptation.
source: Upon strong depolarization, FS cells invariably reached steady-state firing rates of 150–300 Hz and their spike trains showed no or little frequency adaptation, while RS cells typically fired an initial fast doublet, followed by a slower, steady-state firing at <50 Hz (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the electrophysiological properties used to identify cell types.

source: Upon strong depolarization, FS cells invariably reached steady-state firing rates of 150–300 Hz and their spike trains showed no or little frequency adaptation, while RS cells typically fired an initial fast doublet, followed by a slower, steady-state firing at <50 Hz (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the electrophysiological properties used to identify cell types.

source: Extracellular LFPs were recorded using glass micropipettes filled with 0.9% sodium chloride, with a tip broken under visual control (tip diameter ~5 μm, 2–3 MΩ resistance), positioned in the center of the L4 barrel.

source: The extracellular signal was amplified 1000× and low-pass filtered at 1.3 kHz using a differential amplifier (EXT-02F, NPI, Tamm, Germany); 20–100 trials were averaged.

claim: Synchrony is defined as the fraction of spikes co-occurring within a predetermined 'synchrony window' (SW).
source: Given any two spike trains, synchrony is defined as the fraction of spikes in the shorter train occurring within a predetermined 'synchrony window' (SW) before or after a spike in the longer train.
evidence: This is a definition of the synchrony measure used in the analysis.

claim: Chance synchrony is the expected synchrony remaining after shifting each spike in one train by a random jitter ≤J, J being the 'jitter window'.
source: Chance synchrony is the expected (i.e. average) synchrony remaining after shifting each spike in the shorter train by a random jitter ≤J, J being the 'jitter window,' and is calculated analytically rather than by Monte Carlo simulations.
evidence: This is a definition of the chance synchrony measure used in the analysis.

claim: The JBSI is the difference between the observed and chance synchrony, multiplied by a normalization factor β which limits the JBSI to values between 1 (highest possible synchrony) to -1 (lowest possible synchrony), with 0 indicating purely chance synchrony.
source: The JBSI is the difference between the observed and chance synchrony, that is, the magnitude of synchrony destroyed by the jitter, multiplied by a normalization factor β which limits the JBSI to values between 1 (highest possible synchrony) to -1 (lowest possible synchrony), with 0 indicating purely chance synchrony.
evidence: This is a definition of the JBSI measure used in the analysis.

claim: Unlike many other synchrony measures, the JBSI is independent of firing rates and firing rate differentials, and is not sensitive to slow co-modulations in these rates.
source: Unlike many other synchrony measures, the JBSI is independent of firing rates and firing rate differentials, and is not sensitive to slow co-modulations in these rates.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the JBSI measure, supported by a citation.
